entries.subject: Sit the math on a line of its own
entries.body:
The exhaustive formula wraps naturally at the boundaries between what
was multiplied, so on a narrow column it ended up spilling three lines
deep and pulled the deck along with it. It sits under the count now,
which is where it was going to wrap to anyway. Column widths are
pinned, so a longer line stays inside its column rather than shifting
the one beside it.

entries.subject: Let the other three games fold, and spell out the walk
entries.body:
Fold and dead cards move out of HMRDS. Every game now takes a `dead`
pile through the API -- cards out of the deck but belonging to nobody
still in the pot, so they are not scored and take no share, and nothing
unknown can be dealt them either. The URL carries it the same way HMRDS
did, one `dead` entry per folded hand rather than a loose pile, which is
what lets the cards go back into the seat they came out of.

Alongside that, the status line says how the answer came out. When the
walk covers every runout, it labels itself exhaustive and spells out
what it multiplied to get there:

  990 exhaustive runouts (45 × 44 ÷ 2) in 0.002 seconds

A community card is a combination, not a sequence -- the order the flop
comes out in does not matter -- so the ascending product is divided by
the arrangements. The count itself is unchanged and still the truth of
what the answer is built from.

entries.subject: Put the table in the address bar
entries.body:
Every spot now has a URL of its own and comes back from it:

  /holdem/?ranges=KcQc&ranges=Jc6c&board=8h7c2hAd9s

One `ranges` a hand, in seat order, and the board as one run of cards.
HMRDS adds `dead`, one entry per folded hand rather than a loose pile of
cards, which is what lets those cards go back into the seat they came
out of; and a hand checked in but not yet dealt travels as an empty
`ranges`, since five unknown cards is a real state there and counts
against everybody else.

The address bar is written on every change with replaceState, so dealing
a card is not a page the back button has to walk back through. It is
also the one input here somebody else may have written, so cards that
are not cards are dropped and the URL rewrites itself to what was
actually understood: ?ranges=ZZ99&board=Jh__Ts!!2c comes back as
?board=JhTs2c rather than as an error.

entries.subject: Lay the seats out as a list rather than a ring
entries.body:
The ring needed a height settled before anything was dealt: a table with
a fixed aspect ratio, three rows of it, seats pinned to the cells around
the middle one. A board that can run to seven rows has no such height,
so it grew past the box it was given and the seats below went with it --
off the bottom of a page that never got any taller to scroll to them.

The board sits above the seats now and the seats flow as a grid, which
is the shape the narrow screens were already using. All three, since all
three had the ring.

That takes the wide screen block with it, and it is worth naming what
was in there: body height 100dvh with overflow hidden, and every card
sized in cqw against the table as a container. The first is what made
the page unscrollable, and the second is why the cards came out two
pixels wide the moment the table stopped having a width of its own.

entries.subject: Empty a seat that is checked out of the hand
entries.body:
Its cards were released back to the deck but left sitting in the slots,
greyed out, which read as a hand still holding something. They are
cleared now, so checking a seat out says plainly that it was never dealt
in -- and checking it back in gives empty slots to deal into.

Folding is the other case and is untouched: those cards stay where they
are and stay out of the deck. Checking a folded seat out clears it and
puts the fold button back, since a hand that was never dealt cannot have
folded either.

With unchecked seats emptied at the source there is nothing for a
separate list of live slots to leave out, so the deck counts them all
again.

entries.subject: Show the board rows the hand has reached, and drop the frame
entries.body:
Red River keeps thirty one slots because the river can run that far, but
almost every board stops in the first five. The rest stay out of the way
now: a row appears once the row before it is full, and stays for as long
as it holds a card. Clearing the table folds it back to one. A slot in a
row that is not out cannot be dealt into either, so the next card never
lands somewhere nobody can see.

The panel round the ring goes as well, on all three. The seats are boxes
and the felt is a box; a border drawn round the lot of them was a third
frame saying what the first two already did.

entries.subject: Make room on the board for every red card in the deck
entries.body:
Five to a row, and enough rows to hold the longest board the game can
deal. That is 31, not 30: getting all 26 reds onto the river means none
were spent anywhere else, so the flop, the turn and every hole card were
black, and then a black one has to end it. 3 + 1 + 26 + 1. There are
blacks left over to finish on whether two are playing or eight, so it is
a real ceiling rather than a rail, and the engine takes it as one. The
last row holds that final card on its own.

A board that long turned up a bug in the evaluator. The flush test adds
three to each four-bit suit count and reads the top bit, which works
while no count passes twelve -- at thirteen it carries into the next
suit and the flush is lost. Thirteen spades and four diamonds scored as
a high card while holding a royal flush. Reading the counts directly as
well catches it, and costs nothing: a false positive falls through to
the ranks anyway. Seven and eight card hands could never reach it, but
the fix is in all three.

The felt is rounded rather than an oval now. Half of a box seven rows
tall is a pointed arch, which is not what a table looks like.

entries.subject: Stack Red River's board a street at a time
entries.body:
Four rows: the flop, the turn just under it, then the river four to a
row for as long as it ran. Every row centred on the one above.

Five to a row grouped the cards by nothing in particular -- the sixth
card of a board is the second card of the river, and putting it beside
the fifth said otherwise. The turn keeps a tighter gap than the rest, so
it reads as belonging to the flop rather than opening the river.

entries.subject: Let a hand fold without giving its cards back
entries.body:
Unchecking a seat says it was never dealt in, so its cards go back to the
deck for everybody else. Folding is the other thing: the hand is out of
the pot but the cards it was holding are gone, and nobody can be dealt
them. Both now exist, and the checkbox is untouched.

That needed somewhere to put cards belonging to nobody still playing, so
equity takes a dead pile. It is not scored and takes no share, but it
comes off the deck before anything unknown is dealt out of it -- which
is the whole reason for naming those cards. Folding five hearts moves a
two hand pot from 63.5/36.5 to 64.0/36.0, and that gap is the point.

entries.subject: Call it showdown, and fold Red River's board in half
entries.body:
The list is what a hand ends as, which is the showdown rather than the
river -- and on Red River the river is several cards, so naming it that
was wrong twice over. The categories are titled rather than written out
mid-sentence, so they read as the labels they are.

Red River's board also comes down to five slots a row. Ten in a line sat
in the middle column of the ring and set its width, leaving the two
seats above and below it more than twice the width of the rest; the
spread across the eight is 39px now rather than 408.

entries.subject: Add Noah's Ark and Red River, and say what each hand becomes
entries.body:
Two more variants, both Hold'em with a different board, so both reuse
its evaluator.

Noah's Ark turns two community cards a street instead of one: six out by
the river, best five of eight. Six cards flatten the game -- aces over
kings is 78% here rather than 82%, and queens against ace-king is nearer
even than the usual 54/46.

Red River is the awkward one. Its river keeps coming: a red card is
followed by another until a black one ends the hand, so the board
finishes at five cards or six or seven and its runouts are sequences
rather than combinations. Each red that lands opens the deck again, so
the count grows factorially while the probability only halves -- which
is why the walk is only on offer once the board has actually finished,
and why both speeds sample before then. The status line says which.

Every solver now folds out what a hand turns into by the end, royal
flush down to high card, counted over every runout so the column sums to
100%.

That last part turned up a bug in the evaluator that Hold'em could never
have hit. Holding a flush was taken to settle the hand, but the same
cards can make a full house that beats it -- seven cards can never do
both at once, and eight can: 8d 4s 6s 8h 5s 9s 6c 8s is a nine-high
flush and eights full of sixes. Scoring the ranks as well and keeping
the better of the two fixes it, in all three. The flush branch also only
ever scored the longest suit, which stops being the best one once a
board is long enough to carry two of them.

entries.subject: Stop a tapped slot pulling the page in, and deal a hand as it joins
entries.body:
Safari on iOS zooms in on any focused control whose text is under 16px,
and a card slot is 11, so taking a card back off the table zoomed the
page into that hand. The tap no longer hands the slot focus -- the
default on mousedown is blocked -- which is what the zoom was following.
The click still lands, and Tab still focuses a slot the ordinary way, so
the focus listener that arms it keeps working. Hold'em had the same.

Checking a hand in now arms its first empty slot, since checking it in is
asking to deal it. Checking one out goes back to the front of the order,
but to a slot that is free: it used to arm the first slot outright, so
the next card landed on top of whatever was already sitting there.

entries.subject: Fit two hands across a phone, and stop chasing the slot being filled
entries.body:
A seat holds five cards, so at the sizes the page used only one column of
them fitted a phone and the table ran on for screens. Cards, gaps and
padding all come down together below 620px until two columns sit side by
side, and again below 400px; the deck and board come with them.

Arming a slot also focused it, and the browser then dragged that slot
into view -- so dealing a card scrolled the deck you were dealing from
off the screen. Arming is a paint job, and the slots are readOnly, so it
no longer touches the caret. Tapping a slot still focuses it the ordinary
way, which is what the focus listener needs to keep Tab working.

Two things found on the way: the seats nobody had checked were not being
shut until the first card was dealt, because refresh() never ran on load;
and Clear stood 5px taller than the pair above it.

entries.subject: Give Hold'em the same typeface, and a way between the two
entries.body:
Hold'em was still asking for Helvetica and getting Arial on Windows, so
it carries TeX Gyre Heros and the spade now too, and the three pages
finally look like one site.

Each solver also links to the other and back to the front, out at the end
of the title line. The hrefs are root relative, so they resolve against
whatever domain the page is being served from -- which on alexwezensky.com
is the proxy that puts all three behind one name.

entries.subject: Ship the typeface rather than asking for it
entries.body:
Naming Helvetica in a font stack does nothing on a machine that has not
got it, and Windows has not: the stack fell through to Arial, whose a
carries a tail, whose t is cut on the slant, and whose Q and R finish
differently. The page now carries TeX Gyre Heros, a Helvetica drawn from
URW's Nimbus Sans, so the letters are the same everywhere. Nimbus Sans
itself is AGPL and only exempted for PostScript and PDF, which a website
is not; Heros is under the GUST Font License, which is kept beside it.

Also: a spade on green for the tab, Out and Keep now sit above Scoop,
the legend loses its dash and calls the seats hands, and the status line
opens with a capital.

entries.subject: Walk the unnamed cards, and say who is in the pot
entries.body:
The exact walk used to refuse a table with cards nobody had named. It
can walk those too: each way of filling them in is a table with every
hand named, so it is the ordinary walk, and since suits are invisible to
every rule the fillings collapse from card combinations to rank
multisets -- 46,376 ways to deal four unknown cards are 486 walks. That
runs in 10.7s against the 15s the same table took to sample, and answers
exactly rather than closely. Past a thousand fillings there are too many
to beat sampling, so it samples and says so instead of refusing.

Alongside it, seats say whether they are playing. Seat 1 is whoever is
asking and is fixed on; the rest are checked in and out, and a seat that
is out gives its cards back to the deck and drops out of the order deck
clicks fill in. A checked seat needs no cards at all -- whatever it has
not been given is unknown, dealt out of the ranks the board has not
turned, which is to say it has discarded nothing. So four community
cards and two checked seats is enough to solve from.

The divider between Fast and Precise no longer went missing when Precise
was the half selected: the two overlap by a pixel now, rather than one
of them going without a border and hoping its neighbour drew one.

entries.subject: Pin the deck and the column beside it
entries.body:
The status line set the width of the column it sat in, and the deck took
whatever was left, so a longer run of text pulled the column wider and
shuffled the deck along under it. Lengthening one message was enough to
move every card on the page.

Both are given their widths outright -- 470 and 254, which with the gap
is the panel's inner width. A long status now wraps inside its own
column and nothing beside it moves. That also retires the invisible
sizer span, which existed only to hold the column open.

entries.subject: Sample four times as hard when Precise cannot walk
entries.body:
The exact walk cannot deal cards nobody has named -- every way of
filling them in is a different set of live ranks, so each would need its
own walk and none of the work carries over. Precise used to answer those
tables with a red error.

It samples them instead, at a million runouts rather than Fast's quarter
million. Error falls with the root of the trial count, so that halves
it: the spread across seeds drops from 0.06 to 0.02 of a percentage
point, which is what it takes for the last displayed digit to hold
still. It costs about fifteen seconds, which is why only Precise asks
for it.

The status says which it did, so the button does not look ignored.

entries.subject: Let Fast walk the cheap tables, and let the legend breathe
entries.body:
Fast asked for monte-carlo outright, so a settled board was sampled
250,000 times over the two seconds it took, when walking its single
runout is exact and instant. It asks for auto now: the walk when the
walk is affordable, sampling when it is not.

The legend loses its heading, and gains the same gap above it that the
panels have between them -- the seats are a bare grid, so there was no
margin there to inherit.

entries.subject: List a pair as two cards, and put the speed control back
entries.body:
A finished hand was read off the rank mask, which carries one bit per
rank, so a pair came out as a single card: two jacks printed as "J (20)"
and the listing did not account for the total beside it. describe now
takes the seat's own cards and prints one entry each, "J J (20)".

Alongside that, on the page itself:

- Fast and Precise sit above Clear. Fast samples a fixed 250,000
  runouts whatever the table holds; Precise walks every one of them.
- Every figure reads to one decimal place. Equity and Scoop were the
  odd ones at two, which made the same number look like two different
  ones -- an out and a scoop that are always the same runout showed as
  3.0% and 3.03%.
- The stats are spelled out at the foot of the page, which is where the
  instructions used to be at the top.

entries.subject: Deal your own hand before the flop, not after everyone else's
entries.body:
Filling ran straight down the layout -- all ten community cards, then
every seat -- so entering a real spot meant clicking past six board
slots that are not known yet to reach hand 1.

Clicks now travel in the order the table becomes known to somebody
sitting at it: your five, the four community cards that open the game,
then the other seats, with the later streets last. That is not the
dealing order, since everybody is dealt before any community card is,
but it is the order the cards get entered in.

The layout is untouched; fill order is its own list now.

entries.subject: Show dealt cards with their suit pip
entries.body:
Slots read A♠ rather than As, matching the deck they are dealt from.

The slot value was doubling as the card itself, so the pretty version
could not simply be written into it. The canonical card now rides in a
data attribute and cardOf/setCard are the only two places that know the
difference; validation, duplicate checks and the request payload go on
working in As. The pip is a symbol rather than a word, so the slot's
aria-label carries the plain card instead.

entries.subject: Split equity into its high and low halves, and show suits as pips
entries.body:
Each seat now reports the share it takes of each half, ties included.
A pot won outright is never cut in two, so those runouts count towards
neither half -- the gap between the two columns and 100% is how often the
hand ended before it ever reached a showdown.

Card slots show a suit pip rather than a letter, so a slot reads A-spade
the way the deck above it does. The card code lives on the element and
everything downstream still speaks 'As'.

Dealing now runs community cards first and then each seat in turn, which
is the order a hand actually arrives in, and the default sample is
250,000 runouts -- about 0.06% either way, at roughly three seconds.

entries.subject: Rename HMRS to HMRDS
entries.body:
The package, the URLs it serves under, the CLI entry point and every
mention in the docs. The project directory keeps its full name.

entries.subject: Deal HMRS from the deck grid, and read a player by their discards
entries.body:
Ports the Hold'em deck grid: click a card to deal it into the highlighted
slot, click it again to take it back, and the table recalculates itself.
Five card hands and a ten card board will not fit the ring, so seats lay
out as a grid that reflows on its own, with the four streets standing off
from one another on the board.

A hand no longer has to be whole. Whatever hands and discards leave
unnamed is dealt at random each trial, out of the cards that could still
be hidden -- anything the board has matched would be lying face up, so it
is never one of them. That makes a player you can only read by their
discards a player like any other, which is the usual state of things at a
real table. Those cards are drawn before the board, the only order that
leaves both draws uniform, and profiles cache on ranks alone so the
repeated deals cost a lookup rather than a rebuild.

Seats go in once they hold five cards or once anything of theirs is face
up, and a burst of clicks now settles before asking, so dealing a hand
costs one run rather than one per card.

entries.subject: Add an HMRS equity solver
entries.body:
Five card hands, ten community cards turned four/three/two/one, and a
discard every time a community rank matches. Nothing reads a suit, so the
engine runs on 13 bit rank masks and each hand precomputes its surviving
submasks -- survival is one AND and one dict lookup, and scoring is a sum
rather than a five card evaluator.

The exact engine walks only live ranks, the ones somebody holds; every
other rank is interchangeable filler that is counted but never named, so
a memo state is just the remaining count per live rank and the board
falls out of it. Everything from the opening four cards onward is exact
and instant, and auto falls back to sampling for the deal itself.

Both engines settle through one resolve(), checked against a brute force
walk over real cards and against a separate plodding implementation over
4,000 random boards.

entries.subject: Fall back to the list when the window is short, not just narrow
entries.body:
The ring needs room in both directions, so the breakpoint that dropped it
to a list now watches height as well: under 701px there is not enough
column left for three rows of seats worth reading.

Pin the column beside the deck to the width of the longest line it can
ever hold, a seven digit runout count, so a shorter count cannot resize
the deck next to it. In list format that sizer stands down and both the
deck and the column take the full width.

entries.subject: Give every seat its own cell so results cannot collide
entries.body:
Seats were positioned on an ellipse and centred on their ring point, so
their boxes grew both ways as results filled in and adjacent seats ran
into each other and into the board. Eight tall boxes do not fit on a ring
that has to stay inside the window, so the geometry could not be tuned
out of the problem.

The table is a three by three grid now: the board and felt take the
middle cell and the seats ring it clockwise from the top, one to a cell.
Cells cannot overlap, so seats cannot either, whatever the results say.
Each seat carries a border and its own background to read as a box.

Falling out of that, the seat layer is display: contents and no longer a
full size box over the board, so the pointer-events workaround that let
board clicks through is gone with it.

Made hands read as Two pair rather than two pair.

entries.subject: Strip the table down and let clicks reach the board
entries.body:
The seat layer covers the whole table, so it was swallowing every click
aimed at the community cards underneath and they could not be taken back.
It no longer takes pointer events; the seats themselves still do.

Board labels give way to a gap that sets the turn and the river off from
the flop, and the stacked layout gets a little air above it. The deck
hint is gone, Clear and the runout line move into a column beside the
deck, and a slot no longer shows a caret it cannot use.

Equity now reads as Win and Tie on their own lines, and the server
enumerates every runout by default rather than sampling.

entries.subject: Seat 1 at the top, and solve as the cards land
entries.body:
Rotate the ring so hand 1 sits at twelve o'clock and the rest run
clockwise from it.

Drop the Calculate button and the accuracy picker. Every card change now
re-solves once two hands are complete, and the request leaves trials and
mode off so the server's own defaults apply, which is what the picker
selected anyway. A half dealt table is the normal state on this path, so
it waits quietly instead of reporting incomplete input as an error.

Answers can arrive out of order once cards land faster than the server
replies, so each run takes a ticket and stale replies are dropped.

entries.subject: Deal by click only, and keep the table inside the window
entries.body:
Card slots are read only now: cards arrive from the deck, and clicking a
slot that holds one sends that card back to the deck and leaves the slot
armed for the next pick. That drops the typing and paste-chaining code.

The ring layout takes its size from the height the column has left over,
so the 6:5 table always fits without scrolling, and the seats are sized
in container units so they shrink with it instead of colliding.

Also drops the deck heading and the board area's top and bottom padding,
and removes the Railway section from the readme.

entries.subject: Serve the solver at /holdem and tighten the layout
entries.body:
Move the static mount and both API routes under a /holdem prefix so the
bare domain is free for other things, and redirect / there for now. The
Railway healthcheck path follows the route.

Layout: drop the instruction paragraph, lift the deck and the controls
above the table, switch to Helvetica, and scale the chrome to 80%. Hand
seats keep their old size so the hole cards and equity stay readable.
Status line now reads "N runouts in N seconds".

entries.subject: Fall back to port 8080 when PORT is unset
entries.body:
An unset PORT left a bare trailing --port on the uvicorn command, which
exits with an error and crash-loops the service. Default to 8080, the
port the Railway domain routes to.

entries.subject: Deal hands from a card grid around a round table
entries.body:
The page now seats the eight hands on a ring with the board in the middle,
and puts a 52 card deck below it. Clicking a card deals it into the
highlighted slot and moves on to the next empty one, in dealing order:
hand 1, hand 2, flop, turn, river, then hands 3-8. Clicking a card that is
already out on the table takes it back off.

Hand 1's first slot starts selected so the first click has somewhere to go,
and focusing any slot re-aims the deck at it. Typing still works and follows
the same order, because the input list is built in dealing order and doubles
as the fill order. Each seat carries its own equity, bar and made hand;
below 940px the ring falls back to the board on top with the hands stacked
underneath, since the seats need the width.

Drops the "fill in at least two" hint. Calculate still says so if you try.

entries.subject: Move the project readme back up to the repository root
entries.body:
The readme covers the repository as a whole, not PLO8 in particular, so it
belongs beside the game folders rather than inside one of them. Contents are
unchanged; this is a pure rename.

entries.subject: Reorganize PLO8 into a self-contained project folder
entries.body:
Moves the solution, project and sources down a level so PLO8 sits beside
Hold 'em as a self-contained game folder:

  PLO8.sln          -> PLO8/PLO8.sln
  PLO8/PLO8.csproj  -> PLO8/PLO8/PLO8.csproj
  PLO8/Class1.cs    -> PLO8/PLO8/Class1.cs
  README.md         -> PLO8/README.md

The solution's relative reference to PLO8\PLO8.csproj still resolves after
the move. Class1.cs brings along debug changes that were sitting uncommitted
in the working tree: a high-to-low deck fill, nine card deals, reordered
suits, and short rank names.

Also ignores Claude Code's scratch worktrees under Hold 'em/.claude, since
those are a second checkout of this repository rather than project files.

entries.subject: Add Texas Hold'em equity solver
entries.body:
A pure-stdlib engine with a command line tool and a FastAPI web app on top.
Takes up to eight two-card hands and up to five community cards, and reports
each hand's win, tie and overall pot share.

Runouts are enumerated exactly from the flop onward (990 boards on the flop,
44 on the turn), so those answers carry no sampling error. Preflop would be
millions of boards, so it samples by default, with an exact mode available.

Evaluation gives every card a precomputed constant; summing them yields one
integer carrying a count for each rank and each suit. A shared board is summed
once and each player's hole cards are added on top, which keeps an eight-way
preflop simulation under a second in pure Python. A hand's score is a single
int, so comparing hands is > and a chop is ==.

The fast evaluator is checked hand for hand against a deliberately naive one
written separately in the test file, alongside known equities and the usual
edge cases (the wheel, best five of seven, chops, duplicate cards).

Deploys to Railway as a Nixpacks Python service with the root directory set
to this folder.
